source: Facione (1990) Critical Thinking: A Statement of Expert Consensus (APA Delphi Report)
finding: A Delphi panel defined critical thinking for assessment. This definition is the base of the CCTST. It names six core skills: interpretation, analysis, evaluation, inference, explanation, self-regulation.
numbers: 46 experts, six Delphi rounds from Feb 1988 to 1989. Over 95% agreed analysis, evaluation and inference are core. About 87% agreed interpretation, explanation and self-regulation are central.
limits: One assessment expert dissented on interpretation (it is communication, not CT). Another said self-regulation is hard to test with paper and pencil. The panel gives expert opinion, not data.
agent_relevance: Our S0 gate and logs should name which of the six skills each check tests. Self-regulation (checking one's own inferences) is the one tests cannot reach; code-side checks (G2, G3) must cover it.

source: Facione (1990) Delphi report: criteria for judging a CT test (Recommendation 12)
finding: The panel set four criteria for any CT test: content validity, construct validity, reliability, fairness. Items where good thinking gives a wrong answer, or poor thinking a right one, should be removed.
numbers: Recommendation 12 lists 4 criteria. Reliability note: it is unknown whether sub-skills correlate with each other, so test-form reliability figures need caution.
limits: Stated as a standard, not tested. The authors admit sub-skill correlations had not been studied.
agent_relevance: Use these four criteria to audit any benchmark used as a gate. Drop items where a correct answer can come from a bad route (matches G3 and G2).

source: Facione (1990) Delphi report: inventory of tests in print
finding: The report lists tests then in print: Cornell Critical Thinking Tests (Levels X and Z, Ennis and Millman), Ennis-Weir essay test, Test on Appraising Observations (Norris and King, 1983), ACT CAAP (1988), and points to Norris and Ennis (1989) as the guide.
numbers: CAAP CT module: passage-based multiple choice on the ability to clarify, analyze, evaluate and extend arguments. Cornell reviewed in Educ. Psych. Meas. 1983, 43, 1187-1197.
limits: Catalogue only; no psychometric numbers.
agent_relevance: Shows the test formats we can borrow: multiple choice (cheap, code-gradable) versus essay (needs a judge, which G5 limits).

source: Facione (1990) CCTST College Level Technical Report 1: Experimental Validation and Content Validity
finding: The California Critical Thinking Skills Test was built from a bank of 200 piloted items cut to 35 (34 scored). A pre/post comparison in college CT courses found a small but significant gain.
numbers: Pretest n=480 (Feb 1990) mean 16.09/34 (SD 4.65). Posttest n=465 (Nov 1989) mean 16.83 (SD 4.68). Gain 0.74, t=2.44, one-tailed p<.0075. KR-20 .69 pretest and .68 posttest. 18 pretest and 21 posttest sections across 4 courses, 945 students.
limits: Pretest and posttest were different student groups, and the posttest was a course final. The validity argument is partly circular: it assumes the CT courses worked. KR-20 near .68 is low for individual use. Item 26 was dropped.
agent_relevance: A 34-item test with KR-20 .68 gives noisy verdicts. Do not gate S0 on a handful of items; pool many items and report intervals.

source: Facione (1990) CCTST Technical Report 1: item-to-skill map
finding: Items map to skills: 1-5 interpretation, 6-9 analysis, 10-13 evaluation, 14-24 inference, 25-35 explanation. A separate regrouping gives deduction and induction sub-scores.
numbers: Skill groups have 4 to 11 items each. Norris and Ennis (cited) advise reliability of .65 to .75 for multi-skill tests and say very high reliability is not automatically better.
limits: So few items per sub-score means low sub-score reliability (see a11 for measured .21-.51).
agent_relevance: Report only the total score in our logs unless each skill has dozens of items.

source: Facione (1990) CCTST Technical Report 2: Factors Predictive of CT Skills
finding: CCTST scores track general academic aptitude. SAT verbal, SAT math and GPA together predict CCTST; adding the pretest raises the fit further.
numbers: N=1196 subjects over 1989-90. Pretest correlations: GPA r=.20, SAT verbal r=.55, SAT math r=.44, EPT r=.48. R-squared .41 for SAT-V + SAT-M + GPA, and .71 when the CCTST pretest is added.
limits: Correlational; one campus (Cal State Fullerton).
agent_relevance: A CT test overlaps heavily with verbal ability, so a high gate score may only reflect language skill. Add a control with a non-CT verbal test.

source: Facione (1990) CCTST Technical Report 2: language and instructor effects
finding: Non-native English speakers showed virtually no pretest-to-posttest gain, so the author calls CCTST use for this group strongly counter-indicated. Age, units completed and instructor experience added nothing in the main models.
numbers: Non-native speakers were about 19% of the sample. (Report 4 summary in ED337498 gives non-native mean 13.75; native pretest mean 16.65, native posttest 17.59.)
limits: Reading and language load confound the construct, which is the Delphi fairness criterion.
agent_relevance: Prompt wording and reading load can change an LLM's score on a CT item. Keep item language simple and test paraphrases.

source: Facione (1991) Using the CCTST in Research, Evaluation, and Assessment (summary of Technical Reports 1-4)
finding: A control comparison found no natural growth. Students in an Intro Philosophy control did not gain on the CCTST in the same way as students in CT courses.
numbers: Intro Philosophy control: pretest 15.436 vs earlier posttest 15.476, gain +0.04, t=0.08, p=.938 (n=124). Spring posttest 16.356 vs pretest 15.722 (n=90), +0.63, not significant. Norms from 1673 forms: pretest mean 15.89, range 2-29; posttest range 3-31.
limits: The control was one Intro Philosophy course, not a true no-course group. The author asks for replication.
agent_relevance: Measure gain only against a matched no-intervention arm. Our plain arm in bench runs plays this role.

source: Facione (1991) overconfidence among CCTST takers
finding: Students rated their own critical thinking highly while scoring about half. This is a human calibration gap on a CT test.
numbers: Item 'Critical thinking and being logical are quite easy for me': 80% positive (383 of 480) at pretest, 84% (392 of 465) at posttest. Posttest mean 16.83/34 = 49.5% correct.
limits: A single self-report item. Posttest motivation may have been low.
agent_relevance: Same lesson as G1 and G4: self-rated confidence is not evidence. Log correctness separately from stated confidence.

source: Bycio and Allen (2009) The California Critical Thinking Skills Test and Business School Performance
finding: In 131 business students the CCTST correlated with SAT, MFAT-B and GPA, but did not predict the business capstone course better than SAT did. SAT alone explained most CCTST variance.
numbers: N=131 (SAT n=76). SAT alone predicted 56% of CCTST variance. CCTST with MFAT-B r=.63 (n=112); with capstone r=.21, p<.05 (n=97); with overall GPA r=.41 (n=97). SAT-V r=.66 and SAT-M r=.69 with CCTST (n=68). Mean CCTST 20.33 (N=112).
limits: One school, accreditation-driven, low-stakes test, CCTST 2000 version.
agent_relevance: An independent replication of the aptitude overlap. A gate must show what it adds over a plain-model baseline.

source: Liu, Frankel and Roohr (2014) Assessing Critical Thinking in Higher Education: Current State and Directions (ETS RR-14-10)
finding: Review of CCTST, WGCTA, CAAP, EPP, HCTA, CLA+ and others. Main flaws: unreliable sub-scores, non-equivalent forms, unclear differential validity, thin incremental-validity evidence.
numbers: CLA+ constructed-response section reliability .43 (60 min); whole test .87, driven by the 30-min multiple-choice section. CCTST sub-scale alpha .21-.51 (Leppa 1997) vs .68-.70 for the total. WGCTA sub-scale alpha .17-.74 (Loo and Thorpe 1999).
limits: Secondary review; figures come from the cited originals.
agent_relevance: Judge-scored constructed response is the noisy part and code-scored multiple choice the reliable part. Supports G5.

source: Bernard et al. (2008) Exploring the structure of the Watson-Glaser CTA: one scale or many subscales (as cited by Liu et al. 2014)
finding: Liu et al. report that a single-component scale was found across 60 published studies, so WGCTA subscales are not clearly distinct. The original was not opened (publisher redirect).
numbers: 60 studies, as reported by Liu et al. 2014.
limits: Secondhand; not read directly.
agent_relevance: Treat assumption, deduction and inference items as one factor when scoring the agent. Do not claim skill-level diagnosis.

source: Jacobs (1999) and Bondy et al. (2001) on CCTST form equivalence (as cited by Liu et al. 2014)
finding: Liu et al. report CCTST Form B was significantly harder than Form A and that other studies also found low comparability between forms. Originals not opened.
numbers: No figures given in the review.
limits: Secondhand.
agent_relevance: If parallel forms are used for before/after comparisons, equate difficulty first or use the same items in a matched arm.

source: Liu et al. (2014) validity evidence: WGCTA, HCTA and the author-bias problem
finding: WGCTA scores correlated moderately with job performance in one study; HCTA scores related to fewer negative life events. Studies by researchers not tied to a test report lower psychometric quality than studies by its authors.
numbers: Ejiogu et al. (2006) WGCTA vs job performance corrected r=.32 to .52. Butler (2012) HCTA vs negative life events r=-.38. Ku (2009): independent studies report lower quality than author-affiliated ones.
limits: Neither study controlled for general cognitive ability (Kuncel 2011 point), so incremental validity is unknown.
agent_relevance: Validate our gate through someone other than its designer, or through a held-out run.

source: Sternberg (1986) Critical Thinking: Its Nature, Measurement, and Improvement (NIE) - Watson-Glaser section
finding: Describes the Watson-Glaser Critical Thinking Appraisal: five subtests (Inference, Recognition of Assumptions, Deduction, Interpretation, Evaluation of Arguments), two forms of 80 items, optional 40-minute limit, Grade 9 and up.
numbers: Split-half reliability generally in the .70s for the whole test. Correlation with verbally weighted intelligence tests centres near .6.
limits: Sternberg says it is unclear whether the test predicts anything beyond a group intelligence test. This is a review, not new data.
agent_relevance: A model that passes Watson-Glaser is mostly passing a verbal test. It cannot show thinking quality beyond language skill.

source: Sternberg (1986) description of the Cornell Critical Thinking Test
finding: Cornell Level X (71 questions, 50 min, Grade 7+) and Level Z (52 questions, 50 min, college) follow Ennis's conception: induction, source credibility, deduction, assumptions. Level Z adds equivocation, definition, hypothesis testing and gaps in arguments.
numbers: Internal consistency about .8 for Level X and about .7 for Level Z. Correlation with verbal IQ tests around .5. Cornell vs Watson-Glaser r=.48; Cornell vs ACE Test of Critical Thinking r=.44.
limits: Sternberg's verdict: the correlations are 'not auspicious' for a construct apart from general verbal intelligence.
agent_relevance: Cornell sections on source credibility and direction of support for a hypothesis match our G2 and G3 checks and can seed test items.

source: Sternberg (1986) New Jersey Test of Reasoning Skills (Shipman 1983)
finding: A 50-item test claiming to measure 22 skills (conditional syllogisms, dubious authority, causal relations and others). Reported reliabilities mid-to-high .80s; correlates .6 to .8 with New Jersey College Basic Skills Placement subtests.
numbers: 50 items for 22 skill areas, about 2 items per skill.
limits: With about 2 items per skill the skill labels are not measurable. Highly verbal.
agent_relevance: A test that claims many fine skills from few items is a warning sign.

source: Bangert-Drowns and Bankert (1990) Meta-Analysis of Effects of Explicit Instruction for Critical Thinking (AERA)
finding: Instruction in critical thinking raised scores on general CT tests. Of 20 studies, 10 used the Watson-Glaser and 5 the Cornell. Continuous programs beat periodic ones.
numbers: 250 studies collected, 20 usable (19 dissertations). 18 of 20 favoured instruction (8 significant). Mean effect 0.37 SD (50th to 64th percentile). Continuous programs 0.47 vs periodic 0.15. Grades K-8 0.50 vs high school and college 0.21. Content on internal validity only 0.03 vs both internal and external 0.55.
limits: Mostly dissertations. Authors say test gains may not carry over to everyday situations.
agent_relevance: Prompt changes may raise test scores without changing real behaviour. Pair test scores with task outcomes.

source: Kadhi et al. (2010) Watson-Glaser report for 2009-2010 Thurgood Marshall School of Law test takers
finding: Law students scored lower on the post test than the pre test. The evaluator attributes this to unequal administration conditions, not real decline.
numbers: Pre-test N=200 (Aug 2009); 90 took the post test. Median total 59 for matched pre-test takers, 59 for the 110 who skipped the post test, post-test median 50 (a 9-point drop). All paired differences significant and negative; only the AR and AE sub-score pairs correlated pre-post.
limits: Uncontrolled administration and a probably low-stakes post test. Technical report, not peer reviewed.
agent_relevance: Test conditions (stakes, time, instructions) can move scores a lot. Hold the harness identical across arms.

source: Shavelson, Zlatkin-Troitschanskaia et al. (2020) Performance Assessment of Critical Thinking: Conceptualization, Design, and Implementation (Frontiers in Education)
finding: Argues existing CT tests (forced choice, short answer, scenario-based) show moderate to severe construct underrepresentation. Proposes performance tasks built on document portfolios.
numbers: Generalizability coefficient 0.74 for total score with 2 raters and 0.84 with 4 raters. Rater training took 1 day. 60 min was inadequate for the full framework; a full performance task may take 90+ min. CLA+ has a performance task and 25 selected-response items.
limits: About 100k of 105k characters read. No sample sizes or validity correlations in what was read.
agent_relevance: Real critical thinking shows in open tasks with sources; multiple-choice gates miss it. Use a few open tasks plus code checks.

source: OpenAI (2023) GPT-4 Technical Report: exam results
finding: GPT-4 sat the LSAT and other exams. The LSAT is a reasoning test close in spirit to the Watson-Glaser. Instruction tuning helped on some exams and hurt on others.
numbers: LSAT: GPT-4 163 (about 88th percentile), GPT-4 no vision 161 (about 83rd), GPT-3.5 149 (about 40th). SAT EBRW 710/800 (about 93rd). Base vs RLHF GPT-4 on LSAT multiple choice: 67.0% vs 72.0%; SAT EBRW reading 92.3% vs 90.4%; SAT math 57.5% vs 67.5%.
limits: Not the Watson-Glaser itself. Contamination checked only by substring match on question text.
agent_relevance: Top models already beat most humans on human reasoning tests, so such tests are a weak gate for our agent because of ceiling effects.

source: OpenAI (2023) GPT-4 Technical Report: contamination rerun for the LSAT
finding: Exam items found in training data were removed and the exams rerun. For the LSAT the score barely moved.
numbers: LSAT multiple-choice row of the contamination table: 40 questions, 25.00% flagged, difference of -0.85% between full and uncontaminated score.
limits: Substring match uses question text only, so false negatives are possible. The report says RLHF data was not explicitly checked.
agent_relevance: Check every gate item for training-text overlap, and prefer fresh items (G3 style).

source: Zhong et al. (2023) AGIEval: A Human-Centric Benchmark for Evaluating Foundation Models
finding: AGIEval collects 20 human exams, including LSAT (analytical, logical, reading) and LogiQA. GPT-4 beats the average human on LSAT overall but stays weak on analytical reasoning.
numbers: GPT-4 zero-shot: LSAT-AR 35.2, LSAT-LR 80.6, LSAT-RC 85.9, LogiQA-en 49.3. Zero-shot CoT: 34.4, 80.6, 85.1, 57.8. Few-shot: 33.9, 85.9, 87.7, 63.9. Human average LSAT-AR/LR/RC 56, top 91; LogiQA-en human average 86, top 95. ChatGPT zero-shot LSAT-LR 52.6.
limits: CoT lowered LogiQA-Chinese for ChatGPT and GPT-4. Human averages are from published exam statistics.
agent_relevance: Logical-reasoning multiple choice is nearly solved by top models, but constraint puzzles (LSAT-AR) still fail. Our gate should include structured puzzles that need a program check.

source: Liu et al. (2020) LogiQA: A Challenge Dataset for Machine Reading Comprehension with Logical Reasoning (IJCAI)
finding: 8,678 questions from China's National Civil Servants Examination, written by experts to test critical thinking. Models in 2020 were far below people.
numbers: Best 2020 model 35.31% vs human 86.00% (3 post-graduate students) and ceiling 95.00%. Test set 867 pairs. Random guess 25%.
limits: Only three human testers. English version is a translation.
agent_relevance: Civil-service CT tests make good open benchmarks; GPT-4 reached about 50-64% in 2023 (a23), so the gap is closing but not shut.

source: Yu et al. (2020) ReClor: A Reading Comprehension Dataset Requiring Logical Reasoning (ICLR)
finding: 6,138 LSAT and GMAT style logical questions. Models do well on EASY items solvable by option bias alone and poorly on the unbiased HARD set. Humans do about the same on both.
numbers: 91.22% of items from real GMAT/LSAT exams. Split 4,638/500/1,000. Graduate students 63.0% test, 57.1% EASY, 67.2% HARD. RoBERTa-large 55.6% test, 75.5% EASY, 40.0% HARD; best fine-tuned row 65.1% test, 78.9% EASY, 54.3% HARD. EASY = items that 5 models answered correctly in all 4 seeds from options alone.
limits: Small human sample. Pre-LLM models.
agent_relevance: A model can pass a CT test by shortcuts. Strip shortcut-solvable items with an answer-only probe, the same idea as G3.

source: Zhong et al. (2021/2022) AR-LSAT: Investigating Analytical Reasoning of Text
finding: Dataset from LSAT logic-game questions. Fine-tuned transformers sit at chance; a neuro-symbolic parser did somewhat better.
numbers: Human 59.7%; random 20.0%. Test: BERT 21.4%, XLNet 22.5%, RoBERTa 23.1%, ALBERT 23.0%, ARM 30.9%, best row 34.2%. Split 1,585/231/230.
limits: Human figure from a small held-out evaluation. Pre-LLM models.
agent_relevance: Constraint puzzles need an explicit solver; supports the program-checks-model split in the schema.

source: Binz and Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3 (PNAS)
finding: GPT-3 was run on classic reasoning tasks. It solved or erred like humans on vignettes, but small changes broke it. It fell for all three Cognitive Reflection Test items.
numbers: 12 vignette tasks: 6 answered correctly, all 12 human-like. CRT items 1-3: intuitive wrong answer on all 3. Reordered Wason cards and a CRT item with a stated wrong premise produced non-human errors. A cab problem with 15% blue cabs got '20%' for black cabs.
limits: GPT-3 (2022) only. Vignettes may be in training data (authors' caution). Few items.
agent_relevance: Famous test items are unreliable for LLMs because of memorisation. Perturb items (reorder, rewrite) as the authors did.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi and Kosinski (2023) Thinking Fast and Slow in Large Language Models (Nat Comput Sci)
finding: CRT-type trap tasks and semantic illusions across GPT models. Older models fell for traps like people; ChatGPT-4 almost never did. Chain-of-thought cut the trap rate for davinci-003.
numbers: 150 CRT tasks. Correct: humans 38% (41% in the original, n=3,428), davinci-003 5%, ChatGPT-3.5 59%, ChatGPT-4 96%. Intuitive wrong: humans 55%, davinci-003 80%, ChatGPT-3.5 15%, ChatGPT-4 0%. 'Let's use algebra' on davinci-003: correct 5% to 28%, intuitive 80% to 29%. Forcing short answers: ChatGPT-4 correct 95% to 88%, intuitive 0% to 10%.
limits: Authors' own CRT variants; models may have seen the CRT. Semantic illusions: 64% intuitive in their human sample vs 52% in the original.
agent_relevance: Chain-of-thought helps on trap items, but strong models pass trap tests silently, so these items stop discriminating (ceiling).

source: Hagendorff et al. (2023) Study 3: few-shot training of intuition
finding: Giving davinci-003 solved examples of the same CRT type lifted accuracy sharply, showing the 'intuition' on these tasks can be learned by pattern.
numbers: Type 2 tasks: 2% to 92% after 2 examples. Type 3: 12% to 92% after 7. Type 1: 0% to about 78% after 30.
limits: Examples were semantically near-identical to test items, so this may be pattern copying.
agent_relevance: A pass after same-type examples is pattern copying, not thinking. Keep demonstrations out of held-out gate items.

source: Moore et al. (2024) The Base-Rate Effect on LLM Benchmark Performance: Disambiguating Test-Taking Strategies from Benchmark Performance (EMNLP Findings)
finding: Multiple-choice scores mix knowledge with a bias toward certain answer letters. The authors rebuild MMLU so each letter is excluded as correct in turn and score the worst variant (Nvr-X-MMLU).
numbers: MMLU has 15,908 questions over 57 subjects. Cloze: GPT-2 Nvr-A 0.007 vs about 0.33 on other variants; Llama2 Nvr-A 0.560 vs 0.33 on others. Under counterfactual prompting only LLaMa3 beats chance (random = 25%) on Nvr-X.
limits: Small models (under 10B), zero-shot only. Larger models untested.
agent_relevance: Use position-shuffled and answer-excluded variants of any multiple-choice gate and report the minimum over variants.

source: Lin et al. (2024) CriticBench: Benchmarking LLMs for Critique-Correct Reasoning
finding: Tests 17 LLMs on generating, critiquing and correcting answers over 15 datasets in 5 reasoning domains. Critique skill rises in line with generation skill; logic-type tasks are easier to correct; weaker models can beat stronger ones at self-critique.
numbers: 17 LLMs, 15 datasets, 5 domains (math, commonsense, symbolic, coding, algorithmic).
limits: Only the abstract and first page were read; per-model numbers not extracted.
agent_relevance: Matches G2: models critique poorly without real output. Keep critique tests as a separate log, not the gate.

source: Gap note: no LLM study of Watson-Glaser, Cornell or CCTST found
url: n/a (Crossref queries; OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, arXiv API returned 429; WebSearch budget exhausted)
finding: No paper was found that gives the Watson-Glaser, Cornell or CCTST itself to an LLM and reports scores. The gap is unconfirmed because search tools were rate-limited.
numbers: 0 relevant hits in 3 Crossref queries.
limits: Absence of evidence under tool limits. Commercial tests are copyrighted, which discourages publication.
agent_relevance: Treat our own S0 gate scores as first data. Use LSAT-style sets (ReClor, LogiQA, AGIEval) as the open proxy.
